newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African parliament to probe alleged oil scams.
newsitem.headline: S.African parliament to probe alleged oil scams.

text.p: Parliamentary public accounts committee chairman Ken Andrew said on Friday that he planned to probe allegations that the Auditor-General's office had covered up unexplained losses on transfers of strategic oil stocks.

He was reacting to allegations in parliament on Wednesday by Mineral and Energy Affairs Minister Penuell Maduna that more than 170 million rand ($37.7 million) had been "lost" through strategic oil transfers and that Auditor-General Henri Kleuver's office had failed to report this to parliament.
"We should find out if there was an error (by the Auditor- General), and if there was not, then we must call Maduna to account," Andrew told Reuters.

Oil industry observers found Maduna's attitude to Kleuver's office puzzling given the long-standing tension between the Auditor-General and the state's Central Energy Fund (CEF), which for years tried to hide behind the secrecy laws so as not to give proper account of how funds were spent.

During the apartheid years, CEF and the state's Strategic Fuel Fund (SFF) were tasked with securing and storing oil supplies in the face of the oil embargo, which was imposed in 1977 and only lifted just before the first all-race elections in 1994.
"If there had been any way to nail them, he would have," one source said of Kleuver.
Others pointed out that the secrecy laws covering CEF would still have been in place in 1994, legally binding Kleuver even if there was supposed to be a new openness in South Africa.
Kleuver's office was not available for comment on Friday.
Answering a question on behalf of Deputy President Thabo Mbeki in parliamentary question time, Maduna had attacked the post-sanctions activities of the CEF and the SFF.

Maduna said that private auditing firm Price Waterhouse Meyernel had reported on February 7, 1994 that there had been an "unexplained loss of a sum of 170 million rand", but this had never been reported to parliament.

Deputy Auditor-General Bertie Loots had said that an abridged version of the financial statements had been given to parliament because of the secrecy provisions which covered CEF and its subsidiaries at the time.

Maduna questioned the Auditor-General's motives in doing this, claiming that this took place just before the elections and in an era of supposed new transparency after years of secrecy about state oil procurement.
It was for this reason, Maduna said, that he had side-stepped Kleuver's office earlier this year to appoint a private firm of auditors to investigate the missing cash.
Since then, CEF general manager Kobus van Zyl has been suspended pending the outcome of the investigation.
-- Lynda Loxton, Cape Town newsroom +27 21 25-2238 ($ = 4.506 South African Rand)
